hints: Think what forms when a hydrated metal salt dissolves in water, and recall the characteristic pink colour of aqueous cobalt(II).
Consider what NaOH does to an aqua complex, whether OH removes a proton or replaces water, and what colour the cobalt(II) hydroxide precipitate shows.
Think what excess ammonia does to that hydroxide precipitate, whether it dissolves by swapping ligands, and what colour the ammine complex shows.
Distinguish a reaction that forms a solid hydroxide by acid base behaviour from one that swaps one ligand set for another without changing oxidation state.
walkthrough:
Start from solution A**
Dissolving $\text{CoSO}_4$ in water gives the hexaaqua ion, $\text{[Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$. This is a very familiar pink solution. No reaction type is needed for A.

Add NaOH to make solid B**
$\text{OH}^-$ acts as a base toward the aqua complex. It deprotonates coordinated water to give the neutral hydroxide, $\text{[Co(H}_2\text{O)}_4\text{(OH)}_2\text{]}$, often written simply as $\text{Co(OH)}_2$. This appears as a blue precipitate. So this is precipitation, an acid base reaction.

Add excess ammonia to make solution C**
Excess $\text{NH}_3$ redissolves the precipitate by replacing water and hydroxide ligands around $\text{Co}^{2+}$. The product keeps cobalt as +2 but now surrounded by six ammonia ligands: $\text{[Co(NH}_3\text{)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$, straw or yellow brown in colour. Because one ligand set is swapped for another, this is ligand exchange.

Final answer: A = $\text{[Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$, pink
B = $\text{[Co(H}_2\text{O)}_4\text{(OH)}_2\text{]}$ / $\text{Co(OH)}_2$, blue; formation of B = precipitation / deprotonation / acid-base
C = $\text{[Co(NH}_3\text{)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$, straw / yellow-brown; formation of C = ligand exchange

hints: Focus on what ligand is needed to convert an aqua complex into $\text{[CoCl}_4\text{]}^{2-}$ and what reagent supplies a very high concentration of that ligand.
walkthrough:
Supply chloride to swap for water**
To make $\text{[CoCl}_4\text{]}^{2-}$ from $\text{[Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$ you need a large excess of $\text{Cl}^-$ to drive ligand exchange toward the tetrahedral chloro complex. Concentrated $\text{HCl}$ provides that.
Final answer: concentrated $\text{HCl}$

hints: Picture the five 3d orbitals in the free $\text{Co}^{2+}$ ion with no ligands present and decide how their energies compare.
Recall how tetrahedral ligands split the set into two levels, which level holds three orbitals and which holds two, and whether the whole split set lies above or below the free ion level.
walkthrough:
Draw the isolated ion level**
With no ligands, all five 3d orbitals experience the same environment, so draw five short lines or boxes side by side at exactly the same height. Label this as degenerate.

Split and lift for tetrahedral**
When four $\text{Cl}^-$ approach tetrahedrally, electron repulsion raises the energy of all d orbitals. They also split because some d orbitals point more directly at ligands than others. In tetrahedral splitting the pattern is inverted compared to octahedral: two lower and three higher. Draw two lines low and three lines high, but make sure even the lower two sit clearly above the isolated ion level.

Final answer: Isolated $\text{Co}^{2+}$: five 3d orbitals at same energy (degenerate).
Tetrahedral $\text{Co}^{2+}$: split into two sets, three higher and two lower, with all d orbitals higher in energy than in the isolated ion.

hints: Visualise a tetrahedron centred on Co with four Cl atoms, and recall the convention of one wedge coming out, one hashed wedge going back, and two normal lines in the plane.
walkthrough:
Show tetrahedral 3D shape**
Place Co in the centre and draw four $\text{Co-Cl}$ bonds pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron. Use a solid wedge for one bond coming toward you, a hashed wedge for one bond going away, and two ordinary straight lines for the other two bonds. That combination tells anyone reading it that the ion is not square planar but tetrahedral.

Final answer: Central Co bonded to $4 \times \text{Cl}$ in tetrahedral arrangement: one solid wedge $\text{Co-Cl}$, one hashed wedge $\text{Co-Cl}$ and two plain $\text{Co-Cl}$ bonds, approximately $109.5^{\circ}$ apart.

hints: Remember $E^{\ominus}_{cell} = E^{\ominus}_{cathode} - E^{\ominus}_{anode}$ and that a positive value means the overall reaction is feasible, so pair a more positive reduction with a less positive oxidation.
For $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ as oxidant, it must be reduced, so look for a manganese half equation that can be reversed as oxidation with a lower $E^{\ominus}$.
For $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ as reductant, it must be oxidised to $\text{O}_2$, so pair the $\text{O}_2$ / $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ couple as oxidation with a manganese reduction that is more positive.
Combine each chosen pair to write a balanced overall equation and calculate $E^{\ominus}_{cell}$ by subtraction, checking atoms, charge and that only listed species appear.
walkthrough:
Pick the oxidising role**
When $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ oxidises something else, $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ itself is reduced. The reduction $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2 + 2\text{H}^+ + 2\text{e}^- \rightleftharpoons 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ has $E^{\ominus} = +1.78 \text{ V}$. Pair it with oxidation of $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ to $\text{MnO}_2$: $$\text{MnO}_2 + 4\text{H}^+ + 2\text{e}^- \rightleftharpoons \text{Mn}^{2+} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ with $E^{\ominus} = +1.22 \text{ V}$. Subtracting gives $$E^{\ominus}_{cell} = +1.78 - 1.22 = +0.56 \text{ V}$$ and overall $$\text{Mn}^{2+} + \text{H}_2\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{MnO}_2 + 2\text{H}^+$$ The alkaline version using $\text{Mn(OH)}_2$ gives $E^{\ominus}_{cell} = +0.88 - (-0.04) = +0.92 \text{ V}$ with $$\text{Mn(OH)}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{MnO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

Pick the reducing role**
When $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ reduces something else, it is oxidised: $$\text{H}_2\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{O}_2 + 2\text{H}^+ + 2\text{e}^-$$ which is the reverse of $\text{O}_2 + 2\text{H}^+ + 2\text{e}^- \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2\text{O}_2$, $E^{\ominus} = +0.68 \text{ V}$. Pair it with reduction of $\text{MnO}_2$ to $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ at $+1.22 \text{ V}$. Then $$E^{\ominus}_{cell} = +1.22 - 0.68 = +0.54 \text{ V}$$ and overall $$\text{MnO}_2 + 2\text{H}^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{Mn}^{2+} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{O}_2$$ Both $E^{\ominus}_{cell}$ values are positive, so both reactions are feasible.

Final answer: $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ as oxidising agent with $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ / $\text{Mn(OH)}_2$:
$\text{Mn}^{2+} + \text{H}_2\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{MnO}_2 + 2\text{H}^+$, $E^{\ominus}_{cell} = +1.78 - (+1.22) = +0.56 \text{ V}$
OR $\text{Mn(OH)}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{MnO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$, $E^{\ominus}_{cell} = +0.88 - (-0.04) = +0.92 \text{ V}$
$\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ as reducing agent with $\text{MnO}_2$:
$\text{MnO}_2 + 2\text{H}^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{Mn}^{2+} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{O}_2$, $E^{\ominus}_{cell} = +1.22 - (+0.68) = +0.54 \text{ V}$

hints: Recall that no external indicator is needed because excess $\text{MnO}_4^-$ has its own colour, and think what the flask contains just before the first permanent excess appears.
walkthrough:
Watch the self indicating end point**
During the titration $\text{MnO}_4^-$ is decolourised as it oxidises $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$, so the flask stays essentially colourless. The first drop in excess leaves unreacted pale pink $\text{MnO}_4^-$, giving colourless to pale pink.
Final answer: from colourless to pale pink

hints: Start with moles of $\text{MnO}_4^-$ in the $25.0 \text{ cm}^3$ aliquot using $n = cV$ with volume in $\text{dm}^3$.
Use the electron balance, 1 $\text{MnO}_4^-$ gains 5 electrons while each $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ loses 1, to find moles of $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ in that aliquot.
Scale from the $25.0 \text{ cm}^3$ portion up to the full $150.0 \text{ cm}^3$ flask, remembering the flask holds two tablets.
Convert total moles of Fe to mass with $m = n \times 55.8$, halve for one tablet, and express in mg.
walkthrough:
Find moles in the titrated aliquot**
Use $n = cV$: $$n(\text{MnO}_4^-) = 0.0500 \times \frac{18.60}{1000} = 9.30 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$$ This is the amount in the $25.0 \text{ cm}^3$ pipetted sample.

Apply the 1 to 5 redox ratio**
From the half equations, $\text{MnO}_4^-$ needs $5\text{e}^-$ and each $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ supplies $1\text{e}^-$, so: $$\text{MnO}_4^- + 8\text{H}^+ + 5\text{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Mn}^{2+} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O} + 5\text{Fe}^{3+}$$ Hence $$n(\text{Fe}^{2+}) = 5 \times 9.30 \times 10^{-4} = 4.65 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol in } 25.0 \text{ cm}^3$$

Scale to the whole flask then to one tablet**
The flask is $150.0 \text{ cm}^3$, which is $6$ times the aliquot: $$n(\text{Fe}^{2+} \text{ total}) = 6 \times 4.65 \times 10^{-3} = 2.79 \times 10^{-2} \text{ mol}$$ This came from two tablets. Mass for two tablets: $$m = 2.79 \times 10^{-2} \times 55.8 = 1.56 \text{ g}$$ For one tablet halve it: $$m = 0.778 \text{ g} = 778 \text{ mg}$$

Final answer: moles $\text{MnO}_4^-$ in $25.0 \text{ cm}^3 = 0.0500 \times 18.60/1000 = 9.30 \times 10^{-4}$
moles $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ in $25.0 \text{ cm}^3 = 5 \times 9.30 \times 10^{-4} = 4.65 \times 10^{-3}$
moles $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ in $150.0 \text{ cm}^3 = 6 \times 4.65 \times 10^{-3} = 2.79 \times 10^{-2}$
mass Fe in two tablets $= 2.79 \times 10^{-2} \times 55.8 = 1.56 \text{ g}$
mass Fe in one tablet $= 0.778 \text{ g} = 778 \text{ mg}$
